subject: bicycle
reasoning:
I'm planning out a vintage bicycle model as a single TypeScript module, working out how to construct wheels with torus geometry, frame tubes connecting key points, a fork, and handlebars, making sure every reference used is properly defined or imported so the code runs as-is.

I'm mapping out concrete coordinates for the bike: wheel size and placement, wheelbase length, bottom bracket position for the cranks, and the path of the seat tube, top tube, and head tube to form a realistic frame geometry.

Now I'm working out the fork crown and blades connecting the head tube to the front axle, the seat stays and chain stays connecting to the rear axle, and starting on the handlebar stem and curved drop bar shape using a Catmull path.

For the saddle, I'll use a scaled sphere geometry for the leather shape plus a seat post rod connecting it to the frame, then set up the wheels using torus geometries for tyre and rim with spoke rods running from hub to rim.

I need a joint structure so wheels can spin — a root frame joint, then separate wheel joints with their rotation axis set along X so the bone direction allows spinning motion.

For tubes I'll use b.rod for the straight frame members and b.capsule at the joints to hide the seams cleanly. For the wheels, since they roll along Z, their plane is YZ with the torus normal aligned along X — I'm positioning the torus geometry accordingly.

Now I'm working out the hub, spokes, rim, chainring, crank arms, and pedals: using thin rods for spokes between hub and rim points, cylinders rotated to lie along X for hubs, and small cylinders/rods for the chainring and cranks, positioning the crank ends symmetrically on each side of the bottom bracket.

Plotting the chain path as a closed curve approximating a loop around the chainring and rear sprocket, with points offset to the chainring's x position and swept into a thin tube for the chain geometry.

Now I'm considering extras for charm: maybe a front wicker basket using a lathe profile, a small brass bell and headlamp near the fork crown, and possibly fenders using swept arcs along the wheels.

Working out the arc geometry for the fenders, rotating around the X axis so the curve sweeps from the top of each wheel forward or backward to form front and rear fender shapes...

Computing the rear fender arc...

I'm settling on wheel radius dimensions and using a sweep helper to generate the fender tube geometry. Now I'm picking a color palette -- a maroon frame with chrome accents for a vintage look.

I'm defining the remaining colors for tires, leather, brass, wicker, and chain, then adding small sphere lugs at the frame joints and a thin headbadge for detail, plus considering a gold pinstripe along the top tube. I'm also checking that the wheels sit properly on the ground plane so the model doesn't sink below y=0.

I'm now placing the key geometry: wheel axle heights, fork crown and blades running down to the dropouts, the seat tube and seat cluster position, and the seat post and saddle placement with an ellipsoid shape scaled for width and length.

I'm then working out the head tube and steerer placement leading up to the stem, and defining the top tube, down tube, and chainstay capsules that connect the frame's main junctions.

For the seat stays and seat tube, I'm connecting the rear dropout area back up to the seat cluster, then moving to the handlebars -- building a stem capsule and a drop-bar path using a curved sequence of points swept with a thin chrome-colored tube.

I'm now adding a brass bell mounted near the right side of the bar, built as a lathe-dome shape, and placing a simple sphere headlamp near the fork crown for front lighting detail.

For the headlamp, I'll instead use a small chrome/brass cylinder rotated to face forward, giving it a more vintage lamp look. For the front basket, I'm sketching out a lathe profile that flares outward into a bowl shape with a rim, though I still need to position it so it properly sits on the handlebar rather than floating above it.

I'm reconsidering the basket placement since mounting it on drop bars looks odd for this vintage style—it's more typical to mount near the head tube, but that risks clashing with the front wheel. I'll drop the basket idea entirely to reduce risk, and instead add a small leather saddle bag box under the seat, checking its position against the rear wheel's curvature to make sure there's clearance. I'm skipping the rear rack and moving on to designing simple box-shaped pedals attached to the crank arms.

Working out crank and pedal geometry...

I'm finalizing the full ordered point sequence for the closed chain loop, then sweeping a small cylindrical path through them with catmull interpolation, closed and uncapped, in the chain color.

Now I'm working out the spoke geometry for each wheel—14 spokes radiating from hub to rim at radius 0.32, alternating flange offsets for a realistic look, rendered as thin chrome rods. Then I'm setting up the rim and tire as torus shapes with appropriate radii and tube thickness, cream for the rim and black for the tire.

I'll drop the separate rim and just use tyre color "#1e1e1e" with a chrome hub cylinder for each wheel, built via a wheel function with 16 spokes per wheel using rods, keeping part count well under budget, and set the frame to a maroon tone for the tubes.

Now I'm adding brass lug spheres at joints, a head badge sphere, a leather saddle, and naming the build "vintage bicycle," confirming capsule and lathe signatures take radius and color options with rotation specified in XYZ degrees — I'll use a lathe profile for the bell dome and keep everything deterministic without randomness, importing only the needed SDK utilities.

Now I'm placing bar-end grip capsules, rear sprocket and chainring cylinders rotated to align their axes, and a cylindrical lamp rotated to face forward, then sketching a kickstand rod running from the chainstay down to the ground for an authentic vintage touch.

I'm working out the tire torus geometry, fender sweep arc, and fender color, then computing the rotated start position for the front fender arc using trigonometry to position it correctly over the tire.

Rear fender arc confirmed from +35 to -35. Now I'm working out the crank and pedal geometry: crank arm capsules running from the axle center to each offset end, with pedal platforms positioned outward from the crank ends at x offsets scaled by side. Then I'm setting up a small stem capsule positioned near the seat area.

I'm positioning the handlebar stem and bars near the top of the head tube, then adding brass sphere lugs at the head tube and bottom bracket joints, plus a small flattened sphere for the head badge. I'm making sure every part call includes a color and an "at" position so untethered parts default to the root joint, then finishing with the meta export and defining the color palette constants for the frame, chrome, tires, leather, and brass materials before writing out the full code.

Writing frame tube geometry...

Still defining wheel spokes...

Now I'm checking the torus and cylinder rotations align correctly for the wheel geometry, then moving to fenders using swept arcs, the saddle built from a scaled sphere, and a saddle bag positioned just below the seat.

I decide to skip the hanging bag since it would float awkwardly, and instead focus on placing the kickstand attached to the chainstay at the correct angle so its foot touches the ground. I'm also working out the bell's lathed profile mounted near the handlebar, a chrome headlamp with a brass lens, and the pedal crank ends before double-checking the torus geometry parameters.

I verify the tire radius math keeps the bottom just barely touching ground, then plan the handlebar sweep with chrome tubing and grip capsules, confirming spoke and part counts stay reasonable. I trim imports to only what's used, add brass sphere lugs at the head tube, bottom bracket, and seat junctions plus a head badge, and prepare to finalize the code with just a brief explanatory note outside it.
